lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6 you planned a story arc. What is the climax? (The turning point, where the tension is greatest.) Today: craft a narrative with a flashback, telling details and reflection.

A flashback jumps back to an earlier time, to show what led to now. Signal it clearly. Use a time phrase (“Three summers earlier,”) and “had” (“She had never seen the sea”). Then find a way back (“Now, on the cliff,”).
The time order is the order events happened. The story order is the order you tell them. A flashback makes the two different, so the reader pieces the times together.

A telling detail shows more than a sentence of explaining. Not “He was poor”, but “He folded the bus ticket and kept it for the way home.” Use the senses: what can the character see, hear, smell and feel?
Pacing: slow down at the important moment, with short sentences and close detail. Speed through the in-between: “Weeks passed.” Dialogue slows the pace; a summary speeds it up.

Reflection lets the narrator think about what the events meant: “I didn't know then that losing would teach me more than winning.” It turns a list of events into a story with meaning, often near the end.
Transitions signal shifts in time and place: “Meanwhile,”, “Years later,”, “Back at the harbour,”. End with a conclusion that follows from the events and reflects on them.

Try it in the world: in Success Stories in the LIFE tab, the buddies act out true stories of real people. Retell one, opening at its most exciting moment, then flashing back. Next: present with multimedia.

choices: a jump back to an earlier time
a jump to the end of the book
exercises.hint: Flash back: which way in time?
exercises.explain: A flashback jumps back to show earlier events that explain the present.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence shows that Kai is scared, without saying it?
exercises.hint: Look for something you can picture, not a feeling word.
exercises.explain: “Kai's legs would not move” lets the reader see his fear; the others just name it.

exercises.prompt: In a story with a flashback, the story order and the time order are different.
exercises.hint: Think about what a flashback does to time.
exercises.explain: True: the story tells some events out of the order they happened.

exercises.prompt: Match each technique to what it does.
items: flashback
telling detail
reflection
pacing
exercises.hint: Two are about time, one about showing and one about meaning.
exercises.explain: A flashback jumps back; a telling detail shows; reflection thinks about meaning; pacing controls the speed.

exercises.prompt: Look at the two rows. Does this story use a flashback?
exercises.hint: Do the lines between the rows cross?
exercises.explain: True: it opens with Mo winning, then jumps back to his injury: the lines cross where the times swap.

exercises.prompt: A story opens: “The trophy shone on Dev's shelf.” Then it flashes back. Put the events in time order.
items: the trophy goes on his shelf
Dev wins the final
Dev studies old games each night
Dev loses every game for a month
Dev joins the chess club
exercises.hint: The opening is the end; find the earliest event and follow what each one leads to.
exercises.explain: He joins, loses for a month, studies every night, wins the final, and the trophy goes on his shelf: the story's opening.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence slides into a flashback in a story told in the past tense?
choices: Years before, Gran had sailed this coast.
exercises.hint: A flashback in a past-tense story uses “had” with the verb.
exercises.explain: “Had sailed” reaches further back than the story's past, so it opens a flashback.

exercises.prompt: Sort the sentences: showing or telling?
items: Rain drummed on the roof all night.
It was a sad day.
She was nervous.
The room was silent except for the clock.
He was angry.
His knuckles were white on the wheel.
exercises.hint: A sentence that names a feeling tells it; a detail you can picture shows it.
exercises.explain: The silent room, the white knuckles and the drumming rain show; “nervous”, “angry” and “sad” just tell.

choices: Only now do I see what that summer taught me.
We walked to the beach at noon.
The sea was cold and grey.
exercises.hint: Reflection thinks about meaning, not about what happened next.
exercises.explain: It looks back and thinks about what the summer meant; the others only tell what happened.

exercises.prompt: Match each transition to the shift it signals.
items: Meanwhile,
Years later,
Three days earlier,
Back at the harbour,
exercises.hint: Ask where in time or place each one moves the reader.
exercises.explain: “Meanwhile” is at the same time; “Years later” jumps forward; “Three days earlier” jumps back; “Back at the harbour” returns to a place.

exercises.prompt: To slow the pace at an exciting moment, use more detail and short sentences.
exercises.hint: Think of a film in slow motion.
exercises.explain: True: close detail and short sentences stretch the moment, so the reader feels it.

exercises.prompt: Which opening hooks the reader and sets up a flashback?
choices: The rope snapped. It had all begun in May.
This story is about a rope.
Once upon a time there was a rope.
exercises.hint: Look for action first, then a jump back in time.
exercises.explain: “The rope snapped” grabs attention at a key moment; “It had all begun in May” uses “had” to jump back and explain how.

exercises.prompt: Order the parts of a narrative that opens with a flashback hook.
items: a jump back to how it began
a dramatic moment near the end
the events that led up to it
a return to the dramatic moment
a reflection on what it meant
exercises.hint: Hook first, then the past, then back to the moment, then its meaning.
exercises.explain: The hook, the jump back, the events that led there, the return to the moment, and a reflection to end.

exercises.prompt: Which telling detail best shows that the old house was empty for years?
choices: Ivy had grown through the letterbox.
exercises.hint: Look for a detail you can picture that proves it.
exercises.explain: Ivy growing through the letterbox shows that no letters have come and no one has opened the door for a long time.

exercises.prompt: Reflection should list more events in order.
exercises.hint: Is reflection about what happened, or what it meant?
exercises.explain: False: reflection thinks about what the events meant; listing events is just telling the story.

exercises.prompt: Sort the sentences: do they slow the pace, or speed it up?
items: Each step on the ice made a tiny crack.
Her eyes met mine. Neither of us spoke.
By the end of the year, we had moved twice.
Summer came and went.
Weeks passed.
My hand shook. The door creaked.
exercises.hint: Does the sentence cover a long time quickly, or stretch one moment out?
exercises.explain: “Weeks passed”, “By the end of the year” and “Summer came and went” rush through time; the shaking hand, the cracking ice and the silent look stretch a moment.
